A Dyson Swarm, Made Real
Technical notes
    Technical note

    Hardware after 2095

    The first sails fly in the 2050s, but the swarm only becomes large a century later, and every part of it is rebuilt as it ages. So almost nothing that flies is built with today’s parts. Which conclusions survive that, and which turn over?

    From eight studies and an adversarial review in docs/data/future/, summarised in docs/future-tech.md, and the page’s model · October 2026

    In short

    • The design survives and gets simpler. Sails still beat boxes of chips. Today’s fast memory never flies, the boxes shrink to a few per cent of the power, and light guides make each sail one machine.
    • Chips stay cool. Hot transistors spend more energy on every operation. Running chips hot saves no mass and wastes sunlight.
    • Silicon is the only solar cell Mercury can supply, at about 21–22% efficiency.
    • Chip factories set the early pace. The swarm needs a hundred billion times today’s chip output. Factories built in space, using no water, let industry double every 1.9 years.
    • How long sails last decides how big the swarm gets. Short-lived sails, poorly recycled, would stop it at a few per cent of the Sun. The central case, 300 years and 99% recycled, lets it close.
    50×less energy per operation than in 2026
    1–2 GBof radiation-proof memory on each chip
    ~12laser terminals per sail, 50–400 Tbps each
    21.5%solar cell efficiency, made without hydrogen
    1.88 yrfor the whole industry to double
    60×more computing per joule of sunlight than 2026 hardware

    Built with hardware that does not exist yet

    Industry starts from one factory on Mercury in 2050 and doubles until Mercury cannot shed the heat of mining any faster, which happens in 2145 (Taking Mercury apart). Because it grows by doubling, almost everything is built at the end. The swarm reaches a millionth of the Sun only in 2116, one per cent in 2141, and closes in 2361. And since sails are rebuilt as they age, the fleet flying at any moment is young.

    So the page shows one mature era of hardware, with today’s for comparison, plus a pessimistic and an optimistic version of the mature era. Each is a consistent set of assumptions rather than a statistical range.

    Logic: how much energy an operation takes

    The single biggest change is how much energy a chip spends on each operation. Counting the whole system, today’s AI chips spend about 8×10⁻¹⁴ joules per operation. The logic study expects about 10⁻¹⁴ by 2040, from smaller transistors, lower-precision arithmetic and memory stacked right on the logic; about 2.6×10⁻¹⁵ by 2070; and 1.4×10⁻¹⁵ after 2100. That is fifty times better than today, and close to the practical floor for conventional logic, about 7×10⁻¹⁶ J.

    That floor is far above the ultimate physical limit. Erasing one bit of information costs at least kT ln 2, about 3×10⁻²¹ J at the chips’ temperature. Real logic stays hundreds of times above that because transistors need about 0.6 volts to switch reliably, and no one expects that to fall much further.

    What about exotic logic?

    Reversible logic recovers most of the energy stored in each switched wire, and could gain several times after 2100. But it trades energy for area: getting g times better costs about 2.4 g² times as much silicon per watt. That caps it at a few times, and multiplies the number of chip wafers needed tenfold or more. It might pay late in the build, once factories catch up; the model leaves it out.

    Superconducting logic, cooled to 4 kelvin, could match silicon’s energy per operation by about 2070, counting the power for its refrigerators. But the refrigerators weigh 6–38 grams per watt, so it computes 20–30 times less per kilogram than the film.

    Better logic does not change the case for the film over boxes, because heat transport decides that. It does raise what each sail computes, and with it the data each sail must move, which is why the mature sail needs light guides in its film and better lasers.

    Why the chips stay cool

    It is tempting to run the chips hot. A hotter film radiates more heat per square metre, so a sail could fly closer to the Sun, catch more light per square metre, and need less film. It does not pay, for a basic reason.

    Every ordinary transistor switches by letting electrons hop over an energy barrier, and the warmer it is, the more electrons leak over the barrier when the switch is meant to be off. To keep it switching cleanly, the voltage, and with it the energy per operation, must rise in proportion to the temperature. The energy goes up as the square of the absolute temperature: 12% more at 105 °C than at 85 °C, and nearly five times as much at 500 °C, even for a perfect device. Exotic materials such as silicon carbide or diamond tolerate heat, but they obey the same rule.

    Against that cost, the gain from a hotter sail is small. It flies closer to the Sun and needs less film per watt, but each operation costs more, and the two cancel almost exactly: computing per kilogram stays flat from 85 °C to 150 °C. Computing per unit of sunlight, meanwhile, falls steadily, by 17% at 105 °C and 31% at 125 °C, because hot cells also convert less light. A swarm that ends up catching all the sunlight it can is short of sunlight, not mass, so cool chips win.

    The closed sphere runs its chips at about 155 °C anyway, because enclosing the Sun leaves no cooler place to be, and pays roughly half its computing per watt for it (Closing the sphere). That is a choice made for Earth’s sake, not for the chips’.

    Memory

    Today’s AI chips sit beside stacks of high-bandwidth memory, a fast kind of DRAM. That memory is gone long before the first sail launches: by the 2030s memory is bonded directly on top of the logic. And the film needs no DRAM at all, because radiation decides which memory can fly where.

    A chip on the unshielded film collects 142–466 krad of radiation in ten years, mostly from bursts of energetic particles from the Sun. DRAM and flash storage fail long before that. Pods, which carry thick shielding, cut the dose a hundredfold, so those memories stay in pods. Three newer kinds of memory, which store bits magnetically, in a ferroelectric crystal or as a change in a material’s resistance, survive doses thousands of times higher, keep their data with the power off, and are not upset by a passing particle. They go on the film.

    Stacked on each chip, these memories grow its capacity from 16 MB today to about a gigabyte by 2040 and tens of gigabytes later. Because they draw no power when idle, they also remove the biggest waste of the 2026 design, where memory leaking current in the heat took a tenth to over half of each chip’s power.

    Mercury limits which memories can be made at this scale. It has almost no indium, platinum, ruthenium, tungsten or tellurium, all common in memory today. The swarm’s memory has to be built from oxides of silicon, titanium and zirconium, and from iron and magnesium oxide. Even zirconium runs short if every chip carries tens of gigabytes.

    Moving data

    Wires on a chip do not get much cheaper with time: the energy to send a bit along a millimetre of wire falls only with the square of the voltage, which has nearly stopped falling. Light does not pay by the millimetre. Optical links are expected to fall from about 5 picojoules a bit in today’s products to 0.03 after 2100. That is why light guides go into the film (Chips in the film).

    Between sails, laser terminals improve from a fraction of a terabit a second today to about 400 terabits a second after 2100, limited by the range of wavelengths a laser can use, not by the number of photons. A 10 cm telescope reaches every neighbouring sail; a 30 cm one reaches pods 3,000–5,000 km away. About a dozen per sail weigh a few per cent of it. Today’s terminals, scaled up to a mature sail’s traffic, would outweigh the sail.

    Solar cells

    Silicon is the only solar cell Mercury can make in these quantities. The cells now used on satellites need indium and germanium, and the promising perovskite cells need iodine; Mercury holds enough of either for at most a hundred-thousandth of the Sun. The best silicon cell on Earth reached 27.8% in 2025, but it relies on hydrogen at its surfaces, and Mercury has almost none. Without hydrogen, a silicon cell in space is expected to reach about 21–22%. The model uses 21.5%, less 5% for the thinner film.

    The cell’s efficiency does not set the film’s temperature, as the sail note explains. What helps most is reflecting the quarter of sunlight that silicon cannot use, which lets the sail fly closer to the Sun. Engines or cells that run on heat, the alternatives that like high temperatures, need two to four times the film’s mass per watt once their chips are cooled.

    Chip factories

    Before Mercury’s heat limits anything, chip factories do. At full speed the swarm needs about 10¹⁸ square metres of chips a year. That is about a hundred billion times the world’s entire chip output in 2025.

    Making one factory is not the problem. Growing them as fast as everything else is. Today a chip factory holds about 250 kg of machines for each square metre of chips it makes in a year. An industry that has to build its own factories as it grows pays for every kilogram of them in time: each doubling must also double the factories.

    The arithmetic

    If each kilogram of swarm carries a square metres of chips, and making a square metre a year takes I kilograms of machines, then growing the factories alongside stretches the doubling time from Td to

    Td′ = Td + ln 2 · I · a

    The mature swarm carries 22 mm² of chips per watt and weighs 0.69 g per watt, so a = 0.032 m² per kilogram. With a space factory at I = 40 kg, a one-year doubling becomes 1.88 years. With today’s 250 kg it would be over six.

    The central case assumes chip factories built in space, about six times leaner than today’s. Space helps: vacuum is free, so there is no clean room, no building and no air handling, which together take about 60% of a factory’s electricity on Earth.

    Chemistry is the other problem. Chip-making on Earth uses water at every step and organic chemicals to pattern the chips. Mercury has almost no hydrogen, so neither is possible. The factory has to run dry: silicon refined through a loop of chlorine compounds, etching with chlorine and oxygen gas, coatings laid down from vapour, and patterning without organic resists. It all takes about 1,150 megajoules per kilogram of swarm, mostly for the chips, but that is only 3–5% of what the swarm itself collects.

    How long sails last, and how big the swarm gets

    Sails retire. Whatever is built must keep being rebuilt, and the fleet stops growing when what retires and is not recycled equals what industry can add.

    That ceiling depends very strongly on the assumptions, and it is not a law of physics. With sails lasting ten years and nothing recycled, the swarm would stop at 15% of the Sun. With 15 years and 94% recycled, at about three quarters. Only with lives of a century or more and 99% recycling does it close.

    Why would anyone retire a working sail? Only to replace its chips with better ones, and that is worth it only while chips improve faster than recycling loses material. With 94% recycled and chips improving 1% a year, the best life is about six years; at 0.2% a year, about thirty. Once chips stop improving, which they will long before the sphere closes, only wear decides, and the sail note shows that with repair, wear allows centuries. That is why the central case takes 300 years: it is what physics allows once improvement stops, not what today’s designs give.

    What could still change

    • The enamel on the back of the film. How well a 15 µm enamel radiates has not been measured; it decides whether the film is 0.17 or 0.19 kg/m².
    • Silicon cells without hydrogen above 22%, or a way to harvest the solar wind’s hydrogen, of which the swarm intercepts about 3×10¹⁴ kg a year already at one per cent of the Sun.
    • Reversible logic late in the build, worth up to two or so times per kilogram.
    • Factory productivity and recycling in orbit, which set both the pace and the ceiling.
    What the adversarial review changed

    The first synthesis of these studies bundled several hopeful choices into its central case: an untested chip-printing process, 25% solar cells without hydrogen, pods at 1% of the power, and no limit on Mercury’s rock. The review judged it “partly refuted”. The design held; the headline numbers did not. The model’s central case now follows the review where it mattered most: factories in space at 40 kg per square metre a year, cells at 21.5%, 42% of the rock turned into spacecraft, and a finite planet. Pods at 6% sit between the synthesis’s 1% and the review’s 15%.
